You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.02 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.15 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.01 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL     FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

RESULTS OF YOUR PREVIOUS ROUND:

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load $R_L$ from a piezo harvester.
    *   Requirements: $v_{avg} \ge 1.8V$, $v_{max} \le 3.6V$, $v_{pp} \le 0.02V$, $t_{up} \le 0.15s$, $dv \le 0.01V$.
    *   Piezo: Sinusoidal current source $I_p \sin(2\pi ft)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25-30 nF) and 20 MOhm.
    *   $V_{oc}$ amplitude $\approx 3.2V$ (S1).
    *   Operating conditions S1-S6 cover various load and excitation levels.

    *   Topology: L-C-S (SSHI inverter) + Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) + Zener clamp.
    *   Results: Fails miserably. $v_{avg}$ is around 0.5-2V (mostly below 1.8V). Ripple and settling time are poor.
    *   Wait, look at the circuit:
        *   `L1` (pzp to n1), `S1` (n1 to pzn). This creates an inductor-switch path across the piezo.
        *   `D1..D4` is a Full-Bridge Rectifier (FBR) connected to `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   Wait, the FBR is connected *directly* to the piezo terminals (`pzp`, `pzn`).
        *   When the switch `S1` closes, it creates a resonant circuit with $C_p$. The current flows through $L$ and $S1$. This is a standard SSHI-like inversion.
        *   However, if the FBR is connected in parallel, the rectifier diodes will conduct as soon as the voltage exceeds the diode drop. This might be stealing the energy before the L-C inversion can happen or interfering with the resonant flip.
        *   Actually, in a typical SSHI circuit, the inverter flips the charge on $C_p$ to increase the voltage across the rectifier. But here, the FBR is always "there".
        *   The results show very low $v_{avg}$ (0.9V). This is strange because the FBR alone (Reference Design) did better ($v_{avg} \approx 2.24V$ on S1).
        *   Conclusion: The addition of the $L$-$S$ branch in parallel with the FBR is either killing the efficiency or the timing is wrong. The FBR is likely clamping the voltage to something that prevents the $L$-$S$ inversion from being effective.

    *   Standard FBR (Reference Design): $v_{avg} = 2.24V$ (S1), but ripple is too high (26.2 mV) and startup is too slow (0.269 s). S2 fails $v_{min}$. S3 fails $v_{max}$.
    *   Need:
        1.  Better voltage regulation (prevent $v_{max} > 3.6V$).
        2.  Higher energy extraction (for S2, S4).
        3.  Faster startup (lower $C_{out}$ or more power).
        4.  Lower ripple (higher $C_{out}$ or better regulation).
    *   Wait, $C_{out}$ for FBR was 2.2 uF. The ripple was 26.2 mV. The goal is 20 mV. We are close on ripple for S1.
    *   The main problems with FBR are:
        *   S2 (heavy load): $v_{avg} = 1.76V$ (needs 1.8V).
        *   S3 (strong excitation): $v_{max} = 5.72V$ (needs 3.6V).
        *   S4 (weak excitation): $v_{avg} = 1.51V$ (needs 1.8V).
        *   Startup: $t_{up} > 0.15s$.

    *   **Option 1: SECE (Synchronized Electric Charge Extraction).**
        *   Instead of a full bridge, use a switch to connect the piezo to the storage cap only at the peaks.
        *   Basically: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$.
        *   Or: Piezo $\to$ Switch $\to$ $C_{out}$ (if we use two switches for polarity).
    *   **Option 2: SSHI with better interface.**
        *   The previous SSHI attempted a parallel L-S flip. A better SSHI usually uses a DC-DC converter or a specific switching sequence.
        *   Actually, the "Parallel-SSHI" (the one attempted) should work if the rectifier is only connected *after* the inversion or if the inversion is handled carefully.
        *   But a simpler approach is the **Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI)** where the inductor flips the voltage of $C_p$ and then a diode allows it to charge $C_{out}$.
    *   **Option 3: Improved FBR + Zener.**
        *   FBR alone was close. The Zener clamp prevents $v_{max} > 3.6V$.
        *   But it doesn't solve the power deficit in S2/S4.
    *   **Option 4: Synchronous Rectification.**
        *   Replacing diodes with switches. But we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
    *   **Option 5: Voltage Doubler / Charge Pump.**
        *   Since $V_{oc}$ is only 3.2V, and we need 1.8V - 3.6V, we can't afford too many diode drops.
        *   A full bridge has 2 diode drops ($\approx 0.5V$). $3.2V - 0.5V = 2.7V$. This should be enough for $v_{avg} = 1.8V$.

    *   The "Parallel-SSHI" failed because the FBR was connected to the same nodes as the $L$-$S$ branch.
    *   In a correct SSHI, the inverter ($L$-$S$) flips the voltage across the piezo. This flipped voltage is then rectified.
    *   Correct SSHI structure:
        Piezo (pzp, pzn) $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Out.
        Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ are in parallel with the piezo.
        When $V_{pzp}$ is at a peak, $S$ closes, flipping the charge.
    *   Wait, the previous design *did* have the FBR and the $L$-$S$ in parallel. Why did it fail?
        *   Maybe the $L$ value was too high or $t_{on}$ too long.
        *   Maybe the $L$-$S$ flip was happening, but the energy was being dissipated or the rectifier was clamping the voltage during the flip.
    *   Let's look at the FBR reference again. It failed S2 and S4 on $v_{min}$. This means we *need* more energy extraction. SSHI is the way to go.

    *   Circuit:
        1.  $C_p$ is internal to piezo.
        2.  $L_1$ from `pzp` to `n1`.
        3.  $S_1$ from `n1` to `pzn`.
        4.  `G1` (SYNC) controls $S_1$.
        5.  Full Bridge Rectifier (D1-D4) from `pzp`, `pzn` to `out`.
        6.  $C_{out}$ from `out` to `0`.
        7.  $DZ_1$ Zener from `out` to `0`.
    *   This is exactly what the previous design did. Why did it fail?
        *   $L = 10\text{mH}$. For $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, the resonant period $T = 2\pi\sqrt{LC_p} = 2\pi\sqrt{10^{-2} \cdot 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = 2\pi\sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 2\pi \cdot 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 100\mu\text{s}$.
        *   $t_{on}$ should be $T/2 \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.
        *   The result showed $t_{on} = 49.7\mu\text{s}$. This is correct.
        *   The $v_{avg}$ was very low (0.9V). This suggests the $L$-$S$ circuit was *consuming* power or interfering with the rectifier.
        *   In a real SSHI, the rectifier diodes must be carefully chosen. If the rectifier is too "strong" (low drop), it might clamp the piezo voltage, preventing the $L$ from charging and discharging effectively.

    *   Maybe a **Half-Bridge Rectifier** (since the piezo is a current source, we can't just ground one side, but we can use a center-tapped-like approach? No, the piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`).
    *   Wait, the piezo is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$. This means the total current is $I_{total} = I_p \sin(\omega t) - C_p \frac{dV_{pzp}}{dt}$.
    *   Let's try a simpler **Synchronous Charge Extraction (SECE)**.
        1.  $L$ is not needed for SECE.
        2.  We use a switch to connect the piezo to the output at the peaks.
        3.  Structure:
            Piezo `pzp` $\to$ `S1` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `out`
            Piezo `pzn` $\to$ `S2` $\to$ `D2` $\to$ `out`
            `S1` closes at positive peak, `S2` at negative peak.
            Wait, we need a way to handle the polarity.
            If $S_1$ is closed and $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, $D_1$ conducts.
            This is basically a switched-capacitor rectifier.

    *   Wait, let's try a **Voltage Doubler** or **Charge Pump** if we can. But that's usually for AC sources.
    *   What if we use a **Half-Wave Rectifier**?
        `pzp` $\to$ `D1` $\to$ `out`.
        `pzn` $\to$ `0`.
        (But `pzn` is not necessarily at 0V).

    *   Let's look at the **S2/S4 failure (low $v_{avg}$)**.
        S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$.
        S4: $R_L = 1000\text{k}\Omega, I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$.
        The energy available per cycle is $\int I_p \sin(\omega t) V dt$.
        The FBR reference failed S2 ($v_{avg} = 1.76V$) and S4 ($v_{avg} = 1.51V$).
        This means we are very close! For S2, we need 1.8V, we have 1.76V. Just a 2% increase in efficiency would fix it.

    *   How to increase efficiency over a Full Bridge Rectifier?
        1.  **Reduce diode drops.** Use DSCH (already done).
        2.  **Synchronous Rectification.** Replace diodes with switches.
            We have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs.
            SYNC 1 (`G1`) could control two switches.
            Wait, `SYNC` only controls its *own* switches. No, it says "closes its switches", plural. Let's check: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds". This implies one SYNC can control multiple switches.
            Let's try:
            `S1` (pzp $\to$ out), `S2` (pzn $\to$ out), `S3` (0 $\to$ pzp), `S4` (0 $\to$ pzn).
            `G1` (SYNC): edges="both", phase=0, ton=small.
            Wait, the `SYNC` controller's behavior is: "closes its switches ... at the piezo voltage extrema".
            If `edges="both"`, it closes at both positive and negative peaks.
            At positive peak ($V_{pzp} > 0, V_{pzn} < 0$):
            We want `S1` (pzp $\to$ out) and `S4` (0 $\to$ pzn) to close.
            At negative peak ($V_{pzp} < 0, V_{pzn} > 0$):
            We want `S2` (pzn $\to$ out) and `S3` (0 $\to$ pzp) to close.
            But one `SYNC` can't distinguish between positive and negative peaks if `edges="both"`. It just closes all its switches.
            So we need two `SYNC`s:
            `G1`: `edges="pos"`, controls `S1` (pzp $\to$ out) and `S4` (0 $\to$ pzn).
            `G2`: `edges="neg"`, controls `S2` (pzn $\to$ out) and `S3` (0 $\to$ pzp).
            This is a **Synchronous Full-Bridge Rectifier**. It eliminates the $0.5V$ diode drop!

    *   Now, let's check if this solves the other problems:
        - $v_{min}$ (S2, S4): Yes, removing diode drops will increase $v_{avg}$.
        - $v_{max}$ (S3): Now it might be *too* high. We need the Zener clamp `DZ1` on `out`.
        - Ripple: $C_{out}$ will handle it.
        - Startup: Synchronous rectification is more efficient, so it should start faster.

    *   `S1`: `pzp` $\to$ `out`, `ctrl`: `G1`
    *   `S4`: `0` $\to$ `pzn`, `ctrl`: `G1`
    *   `S2`: `pzn` $\to$ `out`, `ctrl`: `G2`
    *   `S3`: `0` $\to$ `pzp`, `ctrl`: `G2`
    *   `G1`: `edges`: "pos", `ton`: $1\text{ms}$ (max is $0.001$, but we want it to conduct for a while around the peak), `phase`: 0.
    *   `G2`: `edges`: "neg", `ton`: $1\text{ms}$, `phase`: 0.
    *   `Cout`: `out` $\to$ `0`, value $2.2\mu\text{F}$.
    *   `DZ1`: `0` $\to$ `out`, model `DZ33`.

    *Wait, check the `ton`.* In a synchronous rectifier, you don't want a tiny pulse (like in SSHI). You want the switch to be closed for the entire half-cycle. But the `SYNC` only allows `ton` up to $0.001$ (1ms).
    At $f = 100\text{Hz}$, the half-period is $5\text{ms}$.
    A $1\text{ms}$ pulse at the peak will only capture some of the energy.
    Wait, is there a better way?
    If we use `ton = 0.001`, we get 1ms of conduction every 5ms. That's 20% duty cycle.
    Is that enough?
    Let's re-read: "closes its switches for 'ton' seconds... at the piezo voltage extrema".
    If $V_{pzp}$ is a sine wave, the most energy is available around the peaks. But the current is zero at the peaks!
    Wait, the piezo is a *current source* $I_p \sin(\omega t)$.
    The voltage $V_{pzp}$ is the integral of the current.
    $V_{pzp}(t) = \int \frac{I_p \sin(\omega t)}{C_p} dt = -\frac{I_p}{\omega C_p} \cos(\omega t)$.
    The voltage extrema (peaks) occur when $\cos(\omega t) = \pm 1$, which is when $\sin(\omega t) = 0$.
    So the `SYNC` closes the switch when the current is *zero*.
